content:
For types which are maps with some properties, such as RingHom/OrderHom/ContinuousMap, we usually have .id/.comp for the identity morphism and composition.
For types which are maps and their inverse, such as Equiv/AlgEquiv/RelIso/Homeomorph, we usually have .refl/.trans instead.
But for types which are embeddings, which usually means injective functions plus some properties, we're not so consistent.
What makes something an embedding rather than a morphism isn't so objective, but here's what I found:

  • docs#Function.Embedding: refl/trans
  • docs#RelEmbedding: refl/trans
  • docs#InitialSeg: refl/trans
  • docs#PrincipalSeg: trans
  • docs#SimpleGraph.Copy: id/comp
  • docs#SimpleGraph.Embedding: refl/comp
  • docs#FirstOrder.Language.Embedding: refl/comp
  • docs#FirstOrder.Language.ElementaryEmbedding: refl/comp

Personally I prefer we use id/comp everywhere, even for equivs, since we're still composing functions. refl/trans seems more appropriate for Props such as docs#Topology.IsEmbedding (which incidentally uses id/comp).

This would also help avoid annoying questions such as: is docs#SimpleGraph.Copy an embedding because it's an injective function, or does it not count because docs#SimpleGraph.Embedding exists?

So basically the question is: should we rename docs#Function.Embedding.refl / docs#Function.Embedding.trans, or declare them as the convention?

cc @Yaël Dillies

FWIW I found 89 hom-like types with id/comp, 46 equiv-like types with refl/trans, and these exceptions:

  • docs#SimpleGraph.Iso has refl/comp
  • docs#FirstOrder.Language.Equiv has refl/comp
  • docs#RootPairing.Equiv has id/comp

Also path-like types benefit from having both standards, they use "trans" to mean concatenating paths rather than composing them as functions:

  • docs#Path and docs#ContinuousMap.HomotopyWith have refl/trans
  • docs#Homotopy and docs#ContinuousMap.Homotopy have refl/comp/trans

Personally, I strongly prefer the id/comp convention. IMHO it reflects a more "modern" way of doing math by thinking about morphisms rather than equivalence classes. I think the refl/trans/symm pattern is better reserved for structures that do NOT wrap an underlying map between types (e.g. homotopy equivalence docs#ContinuousMap.Homotopy)
Surely homotopy equivalence wraps an underlying map?
My opinion is that refl/trans should stay for things that can be reversed, and be gone for everything else

Edward van de Meent said:

Surely homotopy equivalence wraps an underlying map?

Whoops, I meant to say homotopy between two functions, not homotopy equivalence of spaces.

Yes, but it isn't a function "between f₀ f₁". If I have a H : Homotopy f₀ f₁ then H.toFun is of type [0,1] × X → Y. If I have another G : Homotopy f₁ f₂ then (H.trans G).toFun still has type [0,1] × X → Y. It wouldn't make sense to call this operation Homotopy.comp because you never compose the underlying maps, you concatenate them. Similarly, it doesn't make sense to rename Homotopy.refl to Homotopy.idsince the underlying map isn't an identity map, it's a constant projection (t, x) ↦ x.

Compare that with the example Snir Broshi gives above of Function.embedding α β. In this case, the type is literally just a wrapper around a map α → β. docs#Function.Embedding.trans is literally just composition of functions and docs#Function.Embedding.refl is literally just an identity map. I'd argue that these should be renamed to Embedding.comp and Embedding.id respectively.
So the distinguishing factor isn't "has an underlying map" but "the composition is induced by composition of functions"
